strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: the paper defines a Riemannian metric on the diffusion noise space by pulling back the Euclidean metric through the score function ($G_{x_t} = J_{x_t}^\top J_{x_t}$), which is a clean, training-free, architecture-agnostic construction. This is a fresh and principled connection between recently discovered spectral properties of the score Jacobian and practical interpolation.

Strong positioning relative to prior work: the related work carefully distinguishes latent-space manipulation in VAEs/GANs, Riemannian geometry of DGMs, LERP/SLERP, and density-based approaches (e.g., GeodesicDiffusion), and the motivation for avoiding high-density paths (following Karczewski et al. 2025a) is clearly articulated.

The method requires no retraining or architectural modification and is directly applicable to pre-trained diffusion models, which lowers the barrier to adoption and makes the contribution practically meaningful.

Experiments are reasonably broad and consistent: synthetic 2D C-shaped data, image interpolation on MorphBench(A), Animal Faces-HQ, CelebA-HQ, and video frame interpolation on DAVIS, Human, RE10K. The proposed metric achieves best FID, PPL, RE, and lowest MSE/LPIPS across all three video benchmarks, which is a consistent (if sometimes modest) improvement.

Useful supporting analysis: spectral gap visualizations (Fig. 8) and the study of $\tau$ sensitivity (Fig. 7) give insight into why an intermediate noise level is needed and provide a partial justification for the geometric interpretation.

The paper is generally clear, the contribution list is explicit, and the appendices (DDIM inversion details, prompt adjustment, ablations) provide adequate reproducibility support, with code stated as supplementary material.
weaknesses: The central geometric claim ('geodesics stay within or run parallel to the data manifold') is only heuristically supported. Proposition 1 concerns minimizing $\|Jv\|_2^2$ for a vector of fixed norm, which is an idealized argument; the paper itself acknowledges that in practice $J$ is not symmetric and the right singular vectors are not exactly orthogonal, so the tangent/normal decomposition is only approximate. There is no rigorous guarantee that the resulting geodesics are manifold-aligned.

Improvements over the closest competitor (GeoDiff) are small in several metrics. In Table 2, RE on CA is 0.177 vs 0.888 (ours vs GeoDiff is actually 0.888/1.962 — re-checking, ours 0.177/0.888/1.962 vs GeoDiff 0.188/0.891/1.969), and PPL differences are within a few percent. No error bars, variance estimates, or significance tests are reported, so it is hard to judge whether these gains are meaningful.

Part of the empirical gain may be attributable to the prompt adjustment inherited from Yu et al. (2025) rather than to the metric itself. Although the ablation in Table 4 addresses this, the improvement is not decomposed cleanly — both SLERP and the proposed method change under the adjustment, and the metric's marginal contribution over a prompt-adjusted SLERP baseline is not isolated in the main tables.

The method is restricted to $t>0$ and cannot be used at $t=0$ due to the degenerate Jacobian and ill-defined score off the manifold. Combined with the $\tau$-sensitivity analysis, this makes the approach dependent on a hyperparameter ($\tau\in[0.4T,0.6T]$) whose optimal value is chosen empirically rather than derived.

Computational cost is acknowledged but not quantified. Geodesic computation involves optimizing an energy functional for 500 iterations per pair, which is substantially more expensive than closed-form LERP/SLERP; the paper argues it is comparable to GeoDiff but provides no runtime or memory figures.

Evaluation is limited to interpolation. The introduction frames the metric as enabling broader 'manifold-aware analysis and operations,' but only interpolation and frame interpolation are tested; other natural applications (e.g., clustering, editing, sampling) are deferred to future work, so the generality of the claim is not demonstrated.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: defining a Riemannian metric on the noise space of a pre-trained diffusion model via the pullback of the Euclidean metric through the score function (g = J^T J) is a natural and training-free way to exploit the recently reported link between the score Jacobian's small singular values and the data manifold.

The resulting objective (minimizing the rate of change of the score along the path, Eq. 10-11) is simple, numerically stable, and requires no architectural modification or additional training, which is attractive from a practical standpoint.

The empirical evaluation is broad: a synthetic 2D dataset, three image datasets (MorphBench, Animal Faces-HQ, CelebA-HQ), and three video benchmarks (DAVIS, Pexels Human, RealEstate10K). The video frame interpolation setting provides genuine ground-truth evaluation (MSE/LPIPS), which is stronger evidence than the image setting.

The method achieves best or near-best scores on most reported metrics (FID, PPL, RE, and MSE/LPIPS on video), and the endpoint reconstruction error is consistently lowest, suggesting good endpoint preservation.
The related work section is thorough and situates the method well relative to latent-space manipulation, Riemannian geometry of DGMs, and density-based interpolation.
A reproducibility statement and attached source code are provided, and the appendix documents the experimental setup in reasonable detail.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The paper explicitly states it builds on Stanczuk et al. (2024) and Ventura et al. (2025), who showed that the score Jacobian's small-singular-value subspace approximates the tangent space. Defining g = J^T J is the immediate consequence of that observation, and Proposition 1 (minimizing ||Jv||^2 with fixed ||v|| favors the tangent subspace) is essentially a restatement of the definition of the smallest right singular vector rather than a substantive theoretical result.

The central claim — that geodesics 'stay within or run parallel to the data manifold' — is not directly validated. All quantitative metrics (FID, PPL, PDV, RE, MSE, LPIPS) measure image/interpolation quality, not manifold adherence. The synthetic-dataset metric (standard deviation of the density p(x) along the path, Table 1) is a weak and arguably circular proxy: minimizing the variance of density along a path does not test whether the path lies on the manifold, and it is trivially minimized by any constant-density path.

Comparison fairness is unclear. Section 5.2 does not state whether the prompt adjustment (text-embedding optimization, Appendix B.3) is applied identically to all baselines in Table 2, or only to the proposed method and GeoDiff. Table 4 shows this adjustment substantially changes MSE/LPIPS for SLERP, so the headline numbers may not reflect an apples-to-apples comparison. The margin over GeoDiff on image interpolation is small (e.g., FID MB(A) 27.44 vs 28.70; PPL 0.380 vs 0.402), so the advantage is fragile.

The claim that computational cost is 'comparable' to closed-form and conformal-metric baselines is unsubstantiated: no wall-clock time or memory numbers are reported, and no discussion is given of how the score Jacobian/Jacobian-vector products scale in the 16,384-dimensional Stable Diffusion latent space.

Ablations are thin. There is no study of the metric design itself (e.g., pullback through the decoder to pixel space, or alternative inner products on the score space), no sensitivity analysis for the number of discretization points (fixed at N=10), no study of the number of optimization iterations, and the regularized metric G = J^T J + λI is dismissed based on unspecified 'preliminary experiments'.

The metric is only usable for t > 0, degenerating on clean data, which undercuts the 'data manifold' framing: the method does not actually operate on the data manifold M_0 but on a thickened, noise-corrupted version, and the choice of τ ∈ [0.4T, 0.6T] is empirical rather than principled.

Despite the framing of a general Riemannian metric for diffusion models, the applications are limited to interpolation; other metric-related tasks are deferred to future work, so the broader utility of the metric is not demonstrated.

The claim of 'perceptually more natural' transitions is supported only by automatic metrics and qualitative figures; no human study or statistical significance testing (error bars) is provided for the main comparisons.

strengths: Proposes a novel and principled Riemannian metric on the noise space of diffusion models using the Jacobian of the score function, enabling geometry-aware interpolation without retraining or architectural modifications.
Provides theoretical intuition via Proposition 1 and spectral gap analysis, showing that minimizing the proposed energy encourages geodesics to follow tangent directions of the learned data manifold.

Extensive experiments on synthetic 2D data, image interpolation (MorphBench, Animal Faces-HQ, CelebA-HQ), and video frame interpolation (DAVIS, Human, RE10K) with multiple quantitative metrics and qualitative results.
Clear writing, thorough related work, and good reproducibility practices, including detailed appendices, hyperparameters, and attached source code.
Practical applicability: the method can be applied to pre-trained diffusion models and yields perceptually more natural transitions than naive and density-based baselines.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification relies on idealized assumptions such as an exact score function and symmetric Jacobian; for practical diffusion models, the Jacobian is not symmetric and the manifold decomposition is only approximate, so positive definiteness and manifold alignment are not rigorously guaranteed for all t.

Novelty is potentially limited by the closely related prior/concurrent work of Azeglio & Di Bernardo (2025) on a score-based Riemannian metric for diffusion models; the paper does not sufficiently differentiate its metric and geodesic interpolation from that work.

The comparison baselines are mostly generic diffusion interpolation methods; recent specialized morphing or video frame interpolation methods (e.g., DiffMorpher, LDMVFI) are not compared, even though they could provide stronger context, albeit with additional training.

The method relies on prompt adjustment from Yu et al. (2025) to achieve competitive results; without this adjustment, performance drops below SLERP with adjustment in Table 4, raising questions about the standalone effectiveness of the proposed metric.

Geodesic computation is an optimization initialized with SLERP, and sensitivity to initialization, number of iterations, and the choice of τ is not fully analyzed; computational cost is higher than closed-form interpolation methods.
Image interpolation evaluation lacks ground-truth correspondences, and the reliance on FID/PPL/PDV metrics may not fully capture perceptual naturalness or semantic faithfulness.

strengths: Proposes a simple, training-free Riemannian metric g_{x_t}=J_{x_t}^T J_{x_t} on the noise space, with a clear geometric interpretation via the score Jacobian's spectral gap separating tangent and normal directions.
Shows two complementary uses: geodesic interpolation and metric-based CFG correction; the latter is principled and can be distilled without inference overhead.

Extensive experiments across synthetic 2D, image interpolation (MorphBench, CelebA-HQ, Animal Faces-HQ), video frame interpolation, guidance correction, and LCM distillation, with consistent improvements over LERP/SLERP/NAO/NoiseDiff/GeoDiff/FIM-based baselines.
Ablations study noise level tau, regularization weight lambda, CG iterations, prompt adjustment, and a different SD backbone, supporting robustness and reproducibility.
The paper is generally well-written, with helpful appendices on Riemannian geometry, diffusion preliminaries, and computational costs.
weaknesses: The theory relies on idealized assumptions (exact score, symmetric Jacobian/Hessian, spectral gap). In practice the score Jacobian is non-symmetric, and the vector-Jacobian product is approximated via finite differences under an approximate symmetry assumption; this could affect the geometric claims and descent direction.
The practical positive-definiteness and robustness of the metric are argued empirically rather than proved; no rigorous bounds or error analysis for the finite-difference approximation are provided.
Evaluation is limited to Stable Diffusion v2.x backbones; generalization to DiT, flow-matching, or other modern diffusion/rectified-flow architectures is not demonstrated.
The iterative geodesic interpolation and guidance correction add substantial computation (extra score evaluations / NFE), which may limit practical adoption despite the distillation pathway.

Some experimental details are inconsistent or under-specified: e.g., the main text says no CFG or negative prompts for DDIM inversion/denoising, while appendix C.3 uses a negative prompt; FID/CLIP significance testing procedure is not fully described, and per-image binomial tests may not directly apply to distribution-level FID.

The comparison with GeoDiff/FIM-based methods may be affected by prompt adjustment and hyperparameter choices; an aligned ablation isolating the metric vs. prompt tuning would strengthen the attribution.

strengths: Proposes a novel training-free Riemannian metric on the diffusion noise space by pulling back the Euclidean metric through the score Jacobian, exploiting its tangent-normal spectral structure; the idea is simple and geometrically motivated.
Connects to the manifold hypothesis and existing intrinsic-dimension/spectral-gap literature, and includes a proposition explaining why tangent directions have small metric norm.

Applies the metric to two distinct tasks (geodesic interpolation and CFG correction) with experiments on synthetic 2D data, image interpolation (MorphBench, CelebA-HQ, AFHQ), video frame interpolation (DAVIS, Human, RE10K), and generation with guidance correction.
Paper is generally clear, with algorithm boxes, ablations on tau, lambda, CG iterations, prompt adjustment, and extensive implementation details/prompts that aid reproducibility.
Interpolation results are often best across PPL, PDV, FID, RE, MSE, and LPIPS, and statistical significance is reported.
weaknesses: A serious experimental fairness issue appears in the video-frame-interpolation table: the main results compare the proposed method (with prompt adjustment) against SLERP and FIM-based baselines without that adjustment. The ablation shows prompt adjustment drastically improves these baselines (e.g., SLERP MSE 15.44 to 9.89, FIM 30.17 to 9.76), so the reported margins are inflated and should be recomputed with identical adjustment for all methods.

The guidance-correction validation is weak: FID improvements over CFG are very small (e.g., 14.29 to 13.81 at w=7.5) despite roughly 3x NFE, and the closest related method TCFG (Kwon et al., 2025), which also damps normal/tangential guidance components, is not compared. The claim that this local projection is geometrically grounded is therefore not strongly supported.

Theoretical support is thin: Proposition 1 is close to restating the definition of the tangent space via small singular values; it does not prove that geodesics stay on or near the data manifold at the moderate tau used in practice, where the spectral gap is not sharp. The metric is only positive semi-definite, and positive-definiteness at used timesteps is argued heuristically rather than enforced.

The interpolation metric is computed using a negative-prompt-adjusted difference of scores (eq. 18), which is not itself a valid score function; the geometric meaning of its Jacobian as a data-manifold metric is not justified.

Claims about preserving endpoint probabilities/manifold fidelity for images and videos are not directly measured; evidence is mostly indirect and qualitative, with no ground-truth probability or manifold-distance evaluation.
Missing discussion of limitations, computational overhead, and societal impact; several notational/appendix issues (e.g., duplicated eq. 18, table formatting) reduce clarity.

The practical contribution for guidance correction is limited given the negligible FID gain and added computation; the distillation benefit also requires additional teacher-side correction during training.

strengths: Proposes a training-free Riemannian metric on the diffusion noise space derived from the Jacobian of the score function, with a clear geometric interpretation via tangent-normal decomposition and spectral gap.

Theoretical motivation is solid: Proposition 1 supports why the metric penalizes normal directions and encourages geodesics to remain tangential to the data manifold; connects the construction to score-space energy minimization.

Comprehensive validation across synthetic 2D, image interpolation, video frame interpolation, guidance correction, and distillation; improvements are consistent and often statistically significant across metrics and datasets.
Well-structured paper with helpful figures, clear algorithms, and detailed ablation studies on time τ, regularization λ, conjugate-gradient iterations, and prompt adjustment.

Practical advantages: no additional training or architecture modifications; guidance correction can be distilled into a student model at no additional inference cost; computational cost comparable to other metric-based iterative interpolation methods.
weaknesses: Novelty relative to prior score-based pullback Riemannian geometry (e.g., Diepeveen et al., 2025) and spectral-gap analyses is not fully clarified; the most closely related prior work is cited but not experimentally compared, leaving the incremental contribution somewhat uncertain.

Practical effectiveness relies on an approximate spectral gap in the score Jacobian; the paper visualizes singular values but does not quantify gap separation, failure modes, or correlation between gap strength and method performance.

The implementation uses finite-difference Jacobian-vector products with h = 1e-4 and assumes approximate symmetry of J; approximation error and its effect on geodesics and guidance correction are not rigorously analyzed.

Interpolation is optimization-based (500 iterations) and also uses prompt adjustment, so wall-clock cost is not fully characterized; only NFE is reported, and overhead relative to closed-form methods such as LERP/SLERP remains a practical concern.

Theoretical statements such as geodesics being mapped to straight lines in score space rely on idealized assumptions (exact score, local diffeomorphism, full-rank Jacobian); real-world applicability is argued but not fully formalized.

Guidance correction improvements over CFG++ are modest on MS-COCO, with limited qualitative examples; no human evaluation or evaluation on newer architectures (e.g., flow matching) is provided, and code/implementation details are not released.
No limitations or societal-impact discussion is included, and some hyperparameter choices (τ, λ, prompt adjustment, negative-prompt score treatment) may affect reproducibility and generalizability.
